pr_title: storage: Use prefix iteration for CheckSSTConflicts
pr_body:
Currently we use a regular iterator to iterate on the
reader/engine in CheckSSTConflicts during ingestion,
even though the SST is usually much smaller in size and
sparser in keys than the engine. Given most of the
time we are just re-seeking the engine iterator anyway,
it makes sense to use a prefix iterator to optimize those
seeks to take advantage of bloom filters on any sstables.

I realized my previous comment and the one in https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/66410#issuecomment-988352339 omitted the high-level claim I was trying to make:

The approach we had earlier of alternating seeks is at a high-level algorithmically optimal since it allows us to seek past dense keys on either side where the other side is missing keys. As an extreme example, consider an sst spanning [a,z) where [a,b) are dense in the engine, and no keys in the sst, [b,c) are dense in the sst and no keys in the sst and so on. Alternating `SeekGE` is the optimal way to get through such a worst case. The problem with using `SeekPrefixGE` is that we lose the output key (as you very well know) so we are forced to iterate over the sst, which is good for some situations, but will be worse for others. It may not actually be "worse for others" now because our SeekGEs are not optimized -- fixing that I think puts us on a sounder algorithmic footing.

I realize that the improvement with optimized SeekGEs may not be as much as this PR for the case where the sst side is sparse. For instance, if the sst side has 1 key for every 1000 engine keys, each SeekGE on the engine would roughly skip the following keys on each level: L6 (900 keys), L5 (90 keys), L4 (9 keys), L3 (1 key). L3 will be able to use the Next optimization (and higher levels too), but L4 and L5 won't be (and let's stick with the assumption that L6 has no bloom filters). SeekPrefixGE on L4 and L5 is probably faster than SeekGE (though I am unsure how much slower SeekGE is if the block being seeked to is in the cache). The other thing (in this sst sparseness case) that may make SeekPrefixGE better is that the probability of there being matching keys on both sides is very low (error or idempotent write case). But we may not care about the same level of improvement if we have an algorithm that is universally faster than before -- I don't have an opinion on what improvement is acceptable.

Thoughts?

I echo your concern there. The old solution was more algorithmically optimal in any well-crafted bad case, but I figured this would work better in the average case so I went for it. i convinced myself of that with the relative-sparseness of SST and the overlap-with-recently-ingested-SSTs-in-engine points, but I'm not as convinced about those now and am happy to revert this and explore SeekGE optimizations. Do you have some particular optimizations there in mind?

The other solution could be something that adaptively switches to `SeekPrefixGE` if it finds itself seeking on the engine iterator a lot. I'm imagining logic like we have `itersBeforeSeek` in the MVCC scanner. That could also have corner cases that end up doing worse, but it might actually not be that hard to write and would reduce the space of worst cases with the current solutions.

As it turns out this PR did end up slowign down my own disaggregated storage performance testing. The YCSB import done by `workload fixtures import` is pretty overlappy and makes `CheckSSTConflicts` pop up pretty obviously in CPU benchmarks. Reverting to master before this merge is slightly better, but still fairly slow.

> explore SeekGE optimizations. Do you have some particular optimizations there in mind?

Take a look at the optimization in `Iterator.SeekPrefixGE` that sets `trySeekUsingNext`, and compare it to what we do in `SeekGEWithLimit`. I think a similar optimization could be applied in the latter case. I hadn't bothered because we did not have obvious CockroachDB use cases (and given the relatively cruder optimization in `pebbleMVCCScanner` seemed good enough).

issue_context.title: bulk: adaptively probe into existing data in AddSSTableRequests.checkForKeyCollisions
issue_context.body:
This is an idea that came from @andreimatei during a conversation about recent large-scale IMPORTs.

During IMPORTs, we repeatedly ingest SSTs through `AddSSTableRequests`. These requests set the `DisallowShadowing` flag to `true`, so they must check that none of the keys in their SST overlap with any of the keys in the destination range:

https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/9335ade9ce91ebdab1996d7c818b16df32557ac8/pkg/kv/kvserver/batcheval/cmd_add_sstable.go#L49-L57

For IMPORTs where the source is sorted similarly to the destination index, this behavior is fine because the destination keyspace is always empty so the call to `checkForKeyCollisions` is free. However, for portions of the IMPORT where the source is not sorted like the destination index, as is almost always the case for tables with secondary indexes, this repeat conflict checking on each `AddSSTableRequests` is quadratic and can dominate the cost of the IMPORT. This is especially true when the IMPORT creates high read amplification in the destination range, further slowing down the scan in `AddSSTableRequests`.

As an IMPORT continues, it would seem that the ratio of existing to new data would become larger and larger. Eventually, all `AddSSTableRequests` would begin to set their `IngestAsWrites` flag. But beyond this, the "efficiency" of each `checkForKeyCollisions` call would decrease.

It's possible that once we cross some threshold, it would be more efficient to probe into the range to check for conflicts instead of scanning the new data and the existing data in parallel using two iterators. The useful analogy here is to perform a "hash join" instead of a "merge join" once the ratio of existing to new data crosses some threshold. This optimization may be negated to some degree by the fact that we [seek each iterator](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/9335ade9ce91ebdab1996d7c818b16df32557ac8/pkg/storage/mvcc.go#L3928) in `checkForKeyCollisionsGo` instead of calling next on them (a "zig-zag join", following our analogy). But what this still doesn't give us is the ability to use SST bloom filters to ignore most SSTs in the existing data. The ability to use bloom filters would be particularly important once read amplification grows.

So the proposal here is to take the ratio of `new/existing keys` and maybe the `read amplification` into account in `checkForKeyCollisions` and to switch to a probing mode once we determine that it makes sense to do so.

@adityamaru is this something we have considered?

Epic: CRDB-2556
comments: I wonder if we (storage?) could do something clever and AND the bloom filters from the new and existing files?

Is there an existing representative benchmark that we can profile? If not, would someone be willing to construct one?

I don't understand the "it would be more efficient to probe into the range to check for conflicts instead of scanning the new data and the existing data in parallel using two iterators" -- we are probing when doing SeekGE on the MVCCIterator. What am I missing?

> I don't understand the "it would be more efficient to probe into the range to check for conflicts instead of scanning the new data and the existing data in parallel using two iterators" -- we are probing when doing SeekGE on the MVCCIterator. What am I missing?

We are not using a prefix iterator, so my understanding is that a call to SeekGE will be unable to use bloom filters and will need to establish a merging iterator over every overlapping SST. This dominates CPU profiles during IMPORTs, especially as read amplification grows. Is my understanding correct that if we used a prefix iterator then we would be able to use bloom filters for these probes?

> Is my understanding correct that if we used a prefix iterator then we would be able to use bloom filters for these probes?

Yes.
Though there can be tradeoffs, since bloom filters can have false positives and checking them is not free. A representative benchmark could help us understand this better, and explore possibilities.

@sumeerbhola Can you point me to example of those benchmarks? Are they tests or are they separate things that we run?

cc @vy-ton who mentioned she has a script that hits the slowdown
Closing, as @itsbilal's change in https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/pull/73514 allows us to use bloom filters in `checkForKeyCollisions`, which is the core of what this issue was about.

I unfortunately lost track of this issue. I'm unsure about the value of bloom filters when most of the data is in L6, which don't have bloom filters. The value may be happening from the fact that there are up to 7 files (in each level) to seek (of which 6 are not actually going to be the top of the heap after the seek, so they are already in the seeked position, but we don't know it), and we have not added an optimization to SeekGE to use Next, while we do have such an optimization for SeekPrefixGE.
I think optimizing SeekGE and continuing with the alternating seeks is probably the more universally performant approach (since iterating over all keys in the sst may be slow in some cases).
I've also added some comments to https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/pull/73514#pullrequestreview-825876449

cc: @itsbilal

review_comments: Am I reading this right that the fast-path if the target span is totally empty, where extIter would land above the sst and then sstIter would be exhausted, is gone now? Instead we'll (quickly) seek to every sst key now, right?

Yeah, that fast path is gone. We don't have an alternative (maybe we could also spin up a non-prefix iter and check it once to see if the entire span is empty). The prefix iterator on its own doesn't help us here as it could skip keys.

it seems like a non-prefix iter with an upper bound would be nice to check if the span is literally empty. We might even have one hanging out already in evalAddSSTable that would avoid needing to make a new one?
Added a fast-path check, and re-ran benchmarks. Thanks!

I think it'd be nice to include an extra branch to this benchmark for whether or not the SST keys overlap -- in the overlap=true case it is as-is, but in the overlap=false case it'd e.g. put all the SST keys between two existing keys or something, so that the SST's target span is totally empty.
